name: Elliptic Curve Integrated Encryption Scheme
description: Elliptic Curve Integrated Encryption Scheme (ECIES) is a hybrid public-key encryption scheme that combines Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH), a Key Derivation Function (KDF), symmetric encryption, and message authentication to securely encrypt subscriber identities. In 5G, ECIES is used as the basis for SUCI generation, allowing the UE to conceal the permanent SUPI before transmitting it over the air. It provides strong confidentiality with relatively low computational overhead while remaining compatible with existing 5G security architecture.

best_when: Identity protection is a high priority
avoid_when: Pure anonymity rather than encryption is the primary objective
Metadata privacy is the primary objective

combination_reason: Adaptive Padding improves resistance against traffic analysis.
Dynamic Pseudonyms reduce long-term subscriber tracking.

limitations: Does not inherently prevent long-term tracking

reasoning_support.selection_reason_template: Recommended because it provides standardized and efficient subscriber identity protection with low latency and strong confidentiality.
reasoning_support.avoid_reason_template: Avoid when post-quantum protection or anonymous authentication is required.
reasoning_support.explanation_template: ECIES protects the subscriber identity by encrypting the permanent identifier before transmission while maintaining low computational overhead.

references.title: 3GPP TS 33.501 Security Architecture and Procedures for 5G System

name: Module-Lattice Key Encapsulation Mechanism
description: Module-Lattice Key Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM), formerly known as CRYSTALS-Kyber, is a post-quantum cryptographic key encapsulation mechanism standardized by NIST. It enables two parties to securely establish a shared secret while remaining resistant to attacks from both classical and quantum computers. Within CAPSS, ML-KEM can serve as a quantum-safe alternative to ECIES for protecting subscriber identities and establishing secure communication.

primary_role.title: Post-quantum identity protection
primary_role.description: Primary mechanism for high-threat environments requiring quantum-resistant identity protection and long-term confidentiality.

avoid_when: Very constrained IoT devices are used
Standard commercial deployment with no quantum threat

reasoning_support.selection_reason_template: Recommended because quantum-resistant security is required while maintaining strong identity protection for long-term deployments.
reasoning_support.avoid_reason_template: Avoid when minimizing latency, bandwidth, or computational overhead is more important than quantum resistance.
reasoning_support.explanation_template: ML-KEM establishes a shared secret using post-quantum cryptography, protecting subscriber identities against both classical and future quantum attacks.

references.title: FIPS 203 - Module-Lattice-Based Key Encapsulation Mechanism Standard

name: Adaptive Padding
description: Adaptive Padding is a traffic analysis defense mechanism that inserts dummy packets or delays transmissions to obscure communication patterns. Unlike cryptographic schemes, it does not encrypt user data or identities but instead protects metadata such as packet timing and packet size. It is commonly combined with encryption mechanisms to improve overall privacy against passive network observers.

primary_role.title: Traffic analysis and metadata protection
primary_role.description: Primary mechanism for hiding communication patterns and reducing metadata leakage through adaptive traffic padding.

combination_reason: Adds metadata protection to encrypted communication.

limitations: Effective only when combined with encryption

reasoning_support.selection_reason_template: Recommended because communication metadata requires protection against traffic analysis and long-term tracking.
reasoning_support.avoid_reason_template: Avoid when bandwidth and latency constraints are more important than metadata privacy.
reasoning_support.explanation_template: Adaptive Padding inserts dummy traffic to hide communication patterns, reducing the effectiveness of traffic analysis without modifying encrypted content.

evidence.primary_reference: Shmatikov & Wang - Adaptive Padding for Traffic Analysis Resistance

references.title: Adaptive Padding: Efficient Traffic Analysis Resistance

name: Dynamic Pseudonyms
description: Dynamic Pseudonyms is a privacy enhancement technique that periodically replaces a user's identifier with temporary pseudonyms to prevent long-term tracking. Instead of exposing a permanent identity across multiple sessions, changing pseudonyms makes it significantly harder for attackers to correlate user activities over time. It is commonly used alongside cryptographic mechanisms rather than replacing them.

primary_role.title: Tracking prevention through dynamic identity rotation
primary_role.description: Primary mechanism for preventing long-term subscriber tracking by periodically changing user identifiers and improving unlinkability.

avoid_when: Strong data confidentiality is the primary objective
Authentication without identity exposure is unnecessary
Protection against active attacks is required

unsuitable_conditions: When strong cryptographic confidentiality alone is required

combination_reason: Provides identity encryption and rotating identifiers.
Combines tracking prevention with metadata protection.

limitations: Cannot prevent active attacks by itself
Privacy depends on pseudonym rotation frequency

reasoning_support.selection_reason_template: Recommended because subscriber tracking risk is high and identity rotation significantly improves privacy without introducing noticeable overhead.
reasoning_support.avoid_reason_template: Avoid when confidentiality or authentication is the primary requirement, since Dynamic Pseudonyms only hide identity relationships.
reasoning_support.explanation_template: Dynamic Pseudonyms periodically replace user identifiers, making it difficult for attackers to correlate multiple sessions and track subscribers over time.

name: Identity-Based Encryption
description: Identity-Based Encryption (IBE) is a public-key cryptographic scheme in which a user's unique identity, such as an email address or subscriber identity, acts as the public key. A trusted Private Key Generator (PKG) generates the corresponding private key. This eliminates the need for traditional public key certificates while simplifying secure communication and identity management.

primary_role.title: Certificate-less identity encryption
primary_role.description: Primary mechanism for identity-centric encryption in environments where eliminating traditional certificate management is a priority.

best_when: Trusted Private Key Generator is available

reasoning_support.selection_reason_template: Recommended because certificate management overhead should be minimized while maintaining strong identity-based confidentiality.
reasoning_support.avoid_reason_template: Avoid when quantum resistance, decentralized trust, or very low latency is required.
reasoning_support.explanation_template: Identity-Based Encryption uses a user's identity as the public key, eliminating certificate management while providing strong confidentiality through a trusted Private Key Generator.

name: Group Signatures
description: Group Signatures are cryptographic signature schemes that allow a member of a predefined group to sign messages anonymously on behalf of the group. A verifier can confirm that the signature was produced by a legitimate group member but cannot determine which member generated it. A trusted Group Manager retains the capability to reveal the signer's identity when accountability is required.

primary_role.title: Anonymous authentication with accountability
primary_role.description: Primary mechanism for authenticating members anonymously within trusted groups while preserving traceability when required.

avoid_when: Very low authentication latency is required

limitations: Signature size larger than conventional signatures

reasoning_support.selection_reason_template: Recommended because anonymous authentication is required while maintaining the ability to identify malicious users when necessary.
reasoning_support.avoid_reason_template: Avoid when computational resources are limited or ultra-low latency is required.
reasoning_support.explanation_template: Group Signatures allow authenticated communication without revealing the individual identity of the signer, while enabling trusted authorities to reveal identities when accountability is necessary.

evidence.primary_reference: Chaum and van Heyst - Group Signatures (1991)

name: Zero-Knowledge Proofs
description: Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs) are cryptographic protocols that enable one party (the prover) to convince another party (the verifier) that a statement is true without revealing any additional information beyond the validity of the statement. They provide privacy-preserving authentication by eliminating the need to disclose sensitive secrets such as passwords, cryptographic keys, or subscriber identities.

primary_role.title: Privacy-preserving verification
primary_role.description: Primary mechanism for proving knowledge or identity attributes without revealing the underlying sensitive information.

best_when: Authentication without revealing secrets is required

combination_reason: ML-KEM provides quantum-safe key establishment while ZKP authenticates privately.
IBE secures identities while ZKP authenticates without revealing secrets.
Adaptive Padding protects metadata while ZKP protects authentication.

limitations: Not yet common in mobile networks

reasoning_support.selection_reason_template: Recommended because authentication must be performed without exposing sensitive credentials or subscriber identities.
reasoning_support.avoid_reason_template: Avoid when computational efficiency or ultra-low latency is more important than authentication privacy.
reasoning_support.explanation_template: Zero-Knowledge Proofs allow a user to prove possession of a secret without revealing the secret itself, enabling strong privacy-preserving authentication.

evidence.primary_reference: Goldwasser, Micali and Rackoff - The Knowledge Complexity of Interactive Proof Systems (1985)
